content_voiceover: This diagram maps the DOACs onto the coagulation cascade so you can visualize exactly where each drug acts. On the left, the extrinsic tenase complex, made of tissue factor and factor seven a, generates a small amount of factor Xa. This activates factor nine to nine a, which combines with factor eight a to form the intrinsic tenase complex, producing a much larger burst of factor Xa. This factor Xa, together with factor five a on the phospholipid surface, forms the prothrombinase complex, which converts prothrombin, factor two, into thrombin, factor two a. Now look at where the drugs act. Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban all block factor Xa directly, shown by the red bars hitting the Xa molecules at the prothrombinase complex. Dabigatran, in contrast, blocks thrombin itself, shown by the red bar at factor two a. Notice thrombin normally feeds back to activate factors five and eight, amplifying the cascade, so blocking thrombin shuts down this positive feedback loop entirely.
keypoints: Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, betrixaban inhibit factor Xa
Dabigatran inhibits thrombin, factor IIa, directly
Xa inhibitors act within the prothrombinase complex
Thrombin inhibition also blocks feedback activation of factors V and VIII
keypoint_voiceover: Remember these four points. The xaban drugs, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban, all inhibit factor Xa. Dabigatran instead inhibits thrombin, or factor two a, directly. The Xa inhibitors act within the prothrombinase complex. And blocking thrombin also shuts down its feedback activation of factors five and eight.
